title: Daniel Vargas Castano
text: Daniel Vargas Castano is a PhD candidate in Economics at the University of Texas at Dallas and a Research Assistant at the Education Research Center (ERC), where he analyzes longitudinal administrative data from Texas public schools and universities. His research focuses on education policy, and his work has been featured by the EdWorkingPapers Policy and Practice Series and the Annenberg EdExchange Evidence Hub.

title: About
text: Daniel Vargas Castano is an applied economist whose research examines education policy using longitudinal administrative data from Texas public schools and universities. He conducts this work at the Education Research Center (ERC) at the University of Texas at Dallas, where he completes his PhD in Economics (expected May 2027). His research has been featured by the EdWorkingPapers Policy and Practice Series and the Annenberg EdExchange Evidence Hub, and he has presented at venues including the Southern Economic Conference and the Society for Research on Educational Effectiveness.

title: An Educational Portrait of Young Adult Hispanics in the US: Trends over the Past 20 Years
text:
Using American Community Survey data from 2000 to 2022, this study traces high school completion rates among Hispanics aged 25–29 in the US. Completion rose sharply over the period, from about 59% in 2000 to nearly 88% by 2020, closing most of the historic gap with white and Black young adults. Gains held for both men and women, and were largest among immigrants, particularly those born in Mexico and the Caribbean and those who arrived in the US as children.

title: Closing the Gaps: Dallas ISD’s Opt-Out Policy
text:
In 2019–20, Dallas ISD began automatically placing students who scored at Meets Grade Level or above on the 5th-grade STAAR into honors courses, unless their families opted out. Using statewide administrative data and a synthetic control design, this study estimates the policy’s effect on taking Algebra I before high school. Relative to a synthetic Dallas ISD built from comparable Texas districts, the policy raised early Algebra I enrollment by 11.7 percentage points and completion by 10.5 points. It narrowed the Hispanic–White enrollment gap by 7.6 points, while the change in the Black–White gap was small and not statistically significant. Descriptive analysis suggests that Black students did not benefit as much likely due in part to having fewer students meet the auto enrollment criterion, more students leaving DISD, and fewer non-honors track students taking Algebra I by 8th grade.
Read the working paper (EdWorkingPaper 25-1184)
